text:
Provincial
Court of Newfoundland & Labrador

Grand Bank

File Numbers 0803A‑00257,
0803A-00258, & 0803A-00259

Between            Her Majesty the Queen

And                          Justin Rex Bungay

Decision

What happened

On August 14, 2003, at approximately
10:30 p.m., a report was made to the Burin Peninsula district offices of the
RCM Police of a disturbance then taking place at or near Church Street in Grand
Bank, NL. Constable Wentzell responded, and found some of the crowd had
dispersed, but nonetheless he commenced an investigation into the complaint.

The investigation revealed that the
Accused, while under the influence of alcohol, had approached a group of young
men and women near the local post office. The Accused had singled out three
young black men, who he called “niggers”, and who he suggested were not welcome
to live here in this great Country of ours. The Accused struck one of the
teenagers with a mug that he had been drinking from, causing a laceration to
his face in the area of his right eye, and threatened to “take on” all three of
the young black men, and also poured the contents of the mug over the hair and
clothing of a young woman who was part of the group.

The group of people became outraged
and upset by the Accused’s actions, and he left the area, following which the
young man with the wound to his face was taken to the local clinic, where his
own mother, a doctor at the clinic, had to use three sutures to close the
wound.

On his arrest the next morning, the
Accused gave a cautioned statement, in which he admitted to having been
drinking contrary to his probation conditions, and also to having struck the
young man in the face with the mug. The Accused was then released on an
undertaking, and remained at large until coming before the court on February
11, 2004, then facing two charges of the undertaking. My decision, dated
February 12, on sentence for those breaches of undertaking has since been
reported at
[2004] N.J. No. 39
. Concomitant with the conviction and sentence
for breach of undertaking, pursuant to
section 524(8)
of the
Criminal Code
, I
revoked the undertaking, and so the Accused has been both on remand and also
serving a penal sentence since February 12, 2004.

On February 24, 2004, which was the
date set for trial of the present charges when the Accused had pleaded not
guilty on November 12, 2003, the Accused changed his plea to guilty to charges
of causing a disturbance, assault causing bodily harm, breach of probation by
committing assault, uttering a threat to cause bodily harm, common assault and
breach of probation by consuming alcohol. Charges of assault with a weapon,
uttering threats to others of the group and incitement to hatred were withdrawn
by the Crown.

The matter was then put over pending
the completion of a pre-sentence report, and so on Wednesday, March 24, 2004, I
heard facts and submissions on sentence. I reserved decision until today to
consider the submissions, including the rarely used provision in
section
718.2
(a)(i) of the
Criminal Code
, which expressly mandates that motivation by
bias, prejudice or hate based on race must be considered as an aggravating
factor by the sentencing court.

The positions of the parties

Crown counsel tendered the Accused’s
records from the youth court and from this court, highlighted the history of
eleven prior offences for breach of court order, said that these were racially
motivated offences requiring a strong message of denunciation, reviewed the
pre-sentence report,  and described the Accused as having a poor history of
compliance with the law.

At that point, the Accused called out
loudly the following words from the dock : “that’s bullshit !”.

Constable Anderson went over and
stood next to the Accused, and so Crown counsel continued with submissions
which included a significant period of incarceration, followed by a period of
probation, with conditions about consumption of alcohol and drugs, avoiding
contact with the complainants, and participating in counseling while on
probation.

The Crown reminded me that the
assault causing bodily harm is a primary designated offence , triggering a
D.N.A. order, as well as a firearms order  under
section 110
of the
Criminal
Code
.

Counsel for the Accused quite
properly described the actions of the Accused as having constituted an “ugly,
unsettling, and unpleasant incident”. He also advised that the Accused , who is
twenty-two years old, has a history of psychiatric problems, having been
diagnosed at the age of sixteen years as having a bi-polar disorder with
psychosis. Notwithstanding the difficulties that the Accused has had with the
law as a young person and subsequently as an adult, the Accused was attending school
up until his incarceration in February.

Counsel for the Accused also
recommended further probation, with counseling as recommended by the probation
office for substance abuse issues, and, given the facts that the Accused is
both impecunious and unemployed, asked that the victim fine surcharge be
waived.

When I asked the Accused if he had
anything to say, he said “No”. He did not apologize for having committed these
offences, nor did he apologize for the outburst during submissions by counsel,
when he referred to the Crown’s submissions as “bullshit”.

An appropriate disposition

The Accused presents as
a young man, who at the age of

twenty‑two years has amassed
twenty‑five convictions under the Criminal

Code. His actions demonstrate  his
continued disrespect for the law, especially this

attack of the victim of the assault causing bodily harm
solely because of the colour of the

victim's skin, and his outrageous
outburst in court during proceedings

yesterday.

While he has a
psychiatric disorder, that serves as no excuse, as it was diagnosed six

years ago, and could be controlled
were the Accused open to treatment.

There was a pre‑sentence
report prepared, which I will briefly review, as

it provides some depth of assistance
in arriving at an appropriate

disposition in this case. At page 2
of the report, we are told that in

September, 2003, the Accused enrolled
in courses to complete the Adult Basic

Education course, and was attending
school two days a week up until his

incarceration in February.

On page 4, we learn that
the Accused reports that he does not have any

issues with alcohol or drugs,
describes himself as a social drinker only,

does not see his substance use as
problematic, and could quit at any time.

Attached to the recently
completed report is a copy of a pre‑sentence report

completed in 2002, when the Accused
was only nineteen years old. At page 9

of that report, the Accused was
described  as using alcohol, marihuana and

hashish at least twice weekly, and
that the Accused believed that neither

his use of alcohol or drugs is a
problem. Notwithstanding this, the Accused

was placed on probation on April,
2002, with conditions that prohibited him

from the use, consumption, or
possession of alcohol and non‑prescription

drugs. It is clear from the agreed
facts of the case at Bar that the Accused

was well under the influence of
alcohol at the time that he committed these

offences. However, the Accused told
the author of the more recent report

that "he does not believe he
should be sentenced to jail time for one night

of consuming alcohol", even
though he also told her [at page 8] that he was

"too intoxicated to recall the
incident". One can only agree with the author

of the report when she concludes, at
page 5, that the Accused has little

insight into the effects of his
behaviour.

At page 6 of the recent
report, we find that the Accused did not keep

appointments with Addictions Services
when he was referred there by his

original adult probation officer, and
has advised the author of the report

that he chose not to return to
Addictions Services as he states that his use

is not problematic, but recreational
only. The report goes on to recommend

that the Accused receive services in
relation to his alcohol and drug

consumption. Absent insight on the
part of the Accused into the connection

between his substance abuse and his
commission of criminal offences,

however, quaere the utility of
further referral to Addictions Services ?

At page 7, we are reminded
of the Accused's two convictions for breach of

probation and two convictions for
breach of undertaking, all committed since

the Accused became an adult, and then
we are told that the Accused and his

mother would like to see him serve a
community based sentence. With respect,

in my view the repeated failure of
the Accused to comply with bail

conditions and probation conditions
very seriously undermines the

possibility of a community based
sentence. I am not inclined to ignore the

fact that, with these convictions,
the Accused now has breached court orders

more than a dozen times. To release
him  into the community, nominally under

supervision by a supervisor from over
fifty kilometers away, would in my

view constitute an affront to good
sense, and would undermine the sentencing

goal of encouraging public confidence
in the administration of justice.

Support for this
conclusion is found in the conclusions in the report that

the Accused lacks insight into his
offending behaviour, and does not believe

that he deserves jail time for these
offences.

At page 8, we are told that the
Accused lacks remorse and does not accept

responsibility for his actions, that
community supervision is not serving as

an effective deterrent for his
unlawful behaviour, and that the author of

the report does not support the
Accused as a candidate for community

supervision. This latter point is
most significant, in that the earlier

report, two years ago, at page 11,
described the Accused as a suitable

candidate for both supervised
probation and a community service order. This

means that the Accused has
deteriorated from being suitable to now being

unsuitable for a community based
sentence.

Also of very serious
concern is the fact that the Accused has moved on from

the property related offences
described in his criminal record to these much

more serious violent and racist
crimes.

I will now briefly review
some cases where racism has been an aggravating

factor on sentence.

In Ingram & Grimsdale

(1977)
1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA)
,
35 C.C.C.(2d) 376 (O.C.A.)
, Dubin, J

"It
is a fundamental principle of our society that every

member must respect the
dignity, privacy and person of

the other.  Crimes of
violence increase when respect for

the rights of others
decreases, and, in that manner,

assaults such as occurred
in this case, attack the very

fabric of our society.
Parliament's concern for the

incitement of racial
hatred is reflected in S. 281 of The

Criminal Code
.  An
assault which is racially motivated

renders the offence more
heinous.  Such assaults,

unfortunately, invite
imitation and repetition by others

and incite retaliation.
The danger is even greater in a

multicultural,
pluralistic urban society.  The sentence

imposed must be one which
expresses the public abhorrence

for such conduct and
their refusal to countenance it."

In Lelas,
(1990)
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
,
58 C.C.C.
(3d)568 (O.C.A.)
, the 22 year old accused had

pleaded guilty to three charges of
mischief by having vandalized a

synagogue, a school, and a car with
neo‑nazi type messages and symbols. At

first instance, the Accused had been
sentenced to six months in jail. On

appeal to the Ontario Court of
Appeal, the sentence was doubled to a year in

jail, even though the accused had
expressed remorse and had apologized to

the Jewish community. In his
decision, Houlden, J.A., said as follows:

"When
mischief is racially or religiously motivated and is done to cause

emotional
injury or shock to a particular segment of Canadian society, it

calls
for a far more severe penalty than mischief which is done merely to

damage
property.

A
sentence of six months is not, in my opinion, sufficient to meet the needs

of
general deterrence and to show society's abhorrence of the acts of the

respondent.
If it were not for the fact that Lelas has been released and

must
be reincarcerated, I would have imposed a longer sentence. The message must go
out loud and clear that conduct, such as that engaged in by the respondent,
will not be tolerated in Canadian society, and if it is engaged

in,
it will be met with a severe penalty.

Accordingly,
I would allow the appeal, and increase the sentence to one year concurrent on
each count."

In  Karalapillai
[1995]
O.J. No. 2105
, the Ontario Provincial Court

sentenced a 38 year old first
offender to four months in jail for repeatedly

telephoning hate messages to the
Simon Wiesenthal Centre over a span a four

months. At paragraph 51, the court
said as follows :

"This particular act or actions of the accused,
covering the time period in

questions, was, in addition to the other descriptions
I have attached to it,

cowardly ‑ although he did admit who he was and
gave an address ‑ unprovoked

and not retaliated against.  It was an act that struck
a fear within the

victim, but was also capable of striking fear, terror
and emotional upset

within the working community attached to the Centre in
question.  And if it

is permitted to go unchecked or properly punished, it
could, in my view,

invite imitation and incite retaliation and hence my
reference to the

decision
Regina v. Ingram and Grimsdale
."

These adjectives, i.e.,
cowardly and unprovoked, apply equally to

describing the actions of the Accused
in this case.

In Miloszewski et
al,
[1999]B.C.J. No.2710
, affirmed on appeal at [2001]

B.C.J. No.2765, a case where five
"skin‑heads" had pleaded guilty to

manslaughter for having beaten to
death a sixty‑five year old Sikh named

Nirmal Singh Gill, the British
Columbia Provincial Court said as follows :

"[para149]
As I have found that the Crown has proven

pursuant
to
Section 718.2
(a)(i) of the
Criminal Code
that the accused were

motivated
by bias, prejudice or hate based on Mr. Gill's race, I conclude

that
this crime is the worst type of offence of manslaughter.  However,

based
on the mitigating factors, cited above in relation to each of the

accused,
I conclude that none of them is the worst type of offender."

Sentences of twelve and
fifteen years were upheld on appeal, even though four of the five accused in
that case were first offenders. At first

instance, the court in that case said
that the attack on Gill was "a

cowardly, brutal, racially motivated
and unproked attack". Again, these

adjectives also apply to the case at Bar.

The Accused is not a
first offender: as noted above, he is sliding down the

slope of misbehaviour from property
offences to more serious offences of

violent and hate crimes.
Simultaneously, the Accused has deteriorated from

having been a suitable candidate for
probation two years ago to now being

not suitable for a community based
sentence. Oblivious to his own substance

abuse, he has refused to continue
involvement with Addictions Services.

Despite his history of multiple
breaches of probation orders, he believes

that he should be sentenced to more
probation. He describes the events of

having assaulted a young woman, by
pouring his drink over her, and having

assaulted a young man by  striking
him with a mug, causing a serious wound

which required sutures, and
threatening to get him, and by calling him and

his family "niggers", on a
public street in Grand Bank, while the Accused

was required to keep the peace and
was prohibited from drinking, as "one

night's drinking".

When he was here in
February, at paragraph 14, I said as follows:

"Taking into account the rulings
of the Court of Appeal in R. v. Hendrix

(1999),
1999 CanLII 13907 (NL CA)
,
176 Nfld. & P.E.I.R.
293
,  G.E.R.,
[2001] N.J. No. 293
, and Lewis

[2003] N.J. No. 328
, no further
probation is ordered."

The Accused was sentenced to a short
period of custody and two years

probation on April 10, 2002. On
February 12 of this year, while he was till

subject to the probation order, he
was sentenced to a further sixty days in

custody, and was also remanded
pending reverse onus bail hearing for

February 24, 2004. On that latter
date he pleaded guilty, and has been on

remand since then.

Considering his history
of breaching probation, and recognizing that he

lacks insight into his substance
abuse, it is unrealistic to expect that

serving any term of probation
following release from custody would aid in

the Accused's rehabilitation.

Having ruled out both a
community based sentence and probation following

release, the only tool left for the
court to use to sentence the Accused is

a period of imprisonment, following
which he will be prohibited from

possession of firearms, ammunition,
and the like. In order to arrive at a

just sentence, all relevant factors,
mitigating and aggravating, must be

considered. The court must denounce these racially motivated
crimes in the strongest possible terms, in hopes

that that denunciation might
specifically deter the Accused, and generally

deter other like‑minded people
from similar behavior in the future, while

also serving to protect the public
and encouraging public confidence in the

administration of justice. The Court
is, of course, mindful of the principle

of totality as discussed by the Court
of Appeal in Crocker, and

distinguishes this case from the
cases involving organized racists, in that

there is no evidence that the Accused
acted with any other person or

organization in mind.

Having said that, these
crimes were ignorant, cowardly, racially motivated,

unprovoked, and boldly carried out on
a street in a small town in

Newfoundland, where bigotry and
intolerance is practically unheard of. To

paraphrase Dubin,J.A., this is a case
where "the sentence imposed must be

one which expresses the public
abhorrence for such conduct and their refusal

to countenance it."

As noted above, the
original sentence of six months
imposed on
Lelas
for

vandalism by spray painting a
synagogue, a school, and a car was doubled to a

year in jail by the Ontario Court of
Appeal. It will take more than soap and

water to wash away the damage done by
the Accused in this case to his

victims, and I include in the class
of victims the physician who had to

suture her son's face closed after he
had been attacked by the Accused, and

her other sons, who the Accused
called "niggers", and told them they did not

belong here.

For what the Accused
calls "one night of drinking", he will be sentenced to

a total of one year in jail. That sentence
is made up of the following

parts: for the assault causing bodily
harm, which was clearly motivated by

hate based on race, the sentence is
six months in jail. For having uttered

threats, which were also racially
motivated, the Accused is sentenced to six

months in jail, concurrent. For the
assault on the girl, by pouring his

drink over her, the Accused is
sentenced to thirty days, consecutive. For

having breached his probation by
failing to keep the peace and be of good

behavior by committing the assault
causing bodily harm, the Accused is

sentenced to three months in jail,
consecutive. For breaching his probation

by consuming alcohol, which, while
committed shortly before committing the

violent offences, is a separate
criminal adventure, the Accused is sentenced

to sixty days in jail, consecutive.
For the offence of causing a

disturbance, the Accused is sentenced
to time served since being remanded.

The Accused will provide
a sample suitable for DNA collection, analysis and

storage within 48 hours. For ten
years following release from custody, he

will be prohibited from possession of
firearms, ammunition and explosive

materials. As the Accused is
impecunious, the victim fine surcharges for the

offences are waived.

A final note is required:
readers of this decision should be aware that the

Accused was not cited for contempt
for his outburst during court

proceedings, nor was he sentenced in
any way for that outburst.

Dated at Grand Bank, NL, this 25
th

day of March, 2004.

Porter, P.C.J.

Counsel:

Crown N. Smith

Accused M. Evans
